reason: Involucral bracts and phyllaries spread outward. The examples are correct.
Inflorescences and their branches can be reflexed or deflexed. The examples are correct.
A costa can bear spines. The examples describe spines on the costa.
Hispid is a hair covering of the abaxial surface. The part is the leaf lamina epidermis.
Colour applies to almost any plant part, and the examples are colour values. The part name was blank in the item, so I could not check the part itself.
A spike can be club-shaped.
A perigynium can be lanceolate (lanceoloid). The examples are correct.
The whole plant can be floccose when the indumentum covers all of it, as in 'plants floccose'.

Some examples describe the ovary as longer than something else, which fits. Others describe the stipe or the internode ('long stalked', 'longer than adjacent internode'), which is the wrong part. A rule would need to attach the length to the part named as the subject of the comparison.
Serrate margins are a standard character, and the examples are correct.
Roots can be clustered (aggregated).
Leaflets can be caducous or deciduous. The examples are correct.
Lobes can be curved or incurved.
The presence or absence of a spathe is a normal character. A few examples ('with a tail', 'stipules fused into a spathe') are loose readings.
The examples say ovoid, which is a 3-D shape. PATO ovate is a 2-D outline. This is a wrong reading. Use the FLOPO ovoid class (see the pending ovate/ovoid shape PR) and not PATO ovate.
A pedicel can be striate (longitudinally lined).
Root nodules can be present or absent. Some examples describe a root that has nodules, which is acceptable.
Lobes and their apices can be oblique.
Leaf scars and sheath scars can be prominent. The examples are correct.
Secondary veins can be arched, as in brochidodromous venation.
A disc can be small or minute. The examples are correct.
Thickening is meaningful for a margin or an apex. Some examples are about the margin, not this part, so the part needs a check.
An awn can be plumose (feathery).
A rachis can be terete (round in cross-section).
Petiolules can be twisted ('tordus' in French).
Trichomes can be minute or small.
Ellipsoid corresponds to prolate, and a berry can have that shape.
Involucral bracts can be oblanceolate.
Stipitate and sessile describe how a part is attached, and the examples are correct. The part name was blank in the item.
A seed coat can have a reticulate pattern.
Petals can be semi-erect or suberect.
Involucral bracts can be lanate or lanuginose (woolly).
Leaflets can be spotted or dotted, including with oil glands.
A column can be straight. The part name was blank in the item.
Branches can point forward (antrorse). Only one flora supports this pair, so I am less sure.
Length is meaningful for the part. The examples give lengths and long/short values.
Prickle dimensions are written as length × width.
Peduncles can be twisted or contorted.
A sheath margin can be ciliate. The examples are correct.
Bracts can be longer or shorter than the florets. A few examples are about leaves or sheaths, which is the wrong part.
Bud colour is meaningful. Some examples give the colour of the hairs and name other parts, which is acceptable.
A lemma can be bifid or bifurcate.
Indusia can be large. The examples are correct.
Auricles can be triangular or deltoid.
The adaxial lamina surface can be setose.
Wrong reading. 'Spur' is a synonym of short shoot in PO, but the examples are about a nectar spur (a flower part, as in orchids) parallel to the ovary. Do not map spur to short shoot here.
Petals can be subcircular or subrotund.
The mouth of a moss capsule can be oblique.
An inflorescence or strobilus can be 4-angled. Some examples are about the rachis, which is a different part.
Glands can be rectangular in outline.
Ligules can be flat. The examples are correct.
A peristome can be reduced in size. A more specific value (decreased size) would be better.
The examples say 'sharp-margined' or 'sharp-edged', so the quality belongs to the margin or edge and not to the whole perigynium. Annotate it on the margin.
Hairiness is meaningful for the part, but 'Hairs.' and 'Hairy tufts' are not clean statements.
A fruit can be knobbly or pebbled.
The colour of pollen cones is meaningful. The examples are correct.

The examples describe the base being bulbous or the plant bulb-like, not the whole plant. A rule would need to attach 'base bulbous' to the base or bulb, and keep only 'plant bulbous' for the whole plant.
'Characteristic' is too generic. The examples are lists of alternatives ('glabrous or ciliate'). A rule should split the alternatives into the specific values.
Peduncles can be recurved, including at fruiting.

'Characteristic' is too generic. The examples are lists of alternatives ('smooth or ribbed') and some name other parts, such as margins. A rule should split the alternatives into specific values on the right part.
